title: Quantum computing approach to realistic ESG-friendly stock portfolios
abstract_summary: The paper formulates a discrete Markowitz portfolio theory (DMPT) that accounts for integer stock weights and limited budgets, demonstrates a necessary rescaling of the risk-aversion parameter so discrete solutions converge to continuous ones for large portfolios, and shows that solving the discrete problem directly (using a D-Wave quantum annealer) outperforms naive rounding of continuous solutions for realistic budgets. It also introduces a Wasserstein-based ESG distance metric to constrain portfolios toward better ESG scores and demonstrates the trade-off between return, risk, and ESG-friendliness on EURO STOXX 50 components.
methodology_description: The authors formulate a discrete Markowitz portfolio optimization (DMPT) with integer stock allocations xi ∈ N, a fixed total number of lots Ntot, and an optional budget constraint p^T x ≤ B. They map the continuous Markowitz utility Qc( r, Σ, ϕ ) = (ϕ/2) x^T Σ x - r^T x to a discrete utility Qd by showing the relation ϕd = ϕc / Ntot and use Qd = (ϕc/(2 Ntot)) x^T Σ x - r^T x when solving the discrete problem. Integer variables are encoded into binary variables and the optimization is expressed as an Ising / QUBO problem; this is solved on a D-Wave quantum annealer accessed via the D-Wave Ocean toolchain. Continuous (convex) Markowitz solutions are solved with CVXPY as the classical baseline. To incorporate ESG, they introduce an ESG-distance constraint based on the Wasserstein p-distance between the portfolio’s ESG-score distribution and the ideal best-score portfolio; in practice they use p = 1 and add DESG(1, x) ≤ D as a linear constraint in the discrete problem. They compare: (i) continuous solution rounded to integer share counts (baseline) and (ii) discrete optimum found on the annealer, reporting Euclidean distance between normalized weight vectors, positions in return-volatility space, portfolio compositions, and ESG-distance behavior as Ntot, budget B, risk-aversion ϕc and ESG bound D are varied. Random sampling is used to visualize the efficient frontier.

Convex quadratic optimization (continuous Markowitz via CVXPY)
Wasserstein distance (p-distance, p=1 used) for ESG constraint
frameworks: D-Wave Hybrid Solver for Constrained Quadratic Models (referenced)
experimental_setup: Discrete problems encoded as Ising/QUBO via D-Wave Ocean and solved on a D-Wave quantum annealer; continuous problems solved on classical solver CVXPY. Portfolio inputs: historical returns and covariance from market price data (selected EURO STOXX 50 components) over 2010-01-01 to 2021-01-01; ESG scores from ISS ESG (latest date in period). Experiments vary Ntot, budget B (example B=100000 €), risk-aversion ϕc (examples 8 and 1), and ESG distance bound D.
dataset_used: Historical market prices/returns and covariances for selected stocks (examples: BMW DE0005190003, Deutsche Post DE0005552004, Deutsche Telekom DE0005557508, Infineon DE0006231004; another set: Deutsche Telekom, SAP DE0007164600, Intesa Sanpaolo IT0000072618, EssilorLuxottica FR0000121667). Data period: 1 January 2010 to 1 January 2021. ESG ratings sourced from ISS ESG (grading 4 to 1).
experiment_input: Market price time series for chosen EURO STOXX 50 component stocks over 2010-01-01 to 2021-01-01; returns and covariance matrix Σ computed from these series (details of frequency/return calculation not explicitly stated); per-stock current prices vector p (used for budget constraint); ISS ESG per-stock scores. Example problem sizes: small k=4 asset universes; Ntot varied (examples include 10..10000 in convergence tests; specific runs used Ntot values like 3401 and 4026 and Ntot values 960,1112,1202,1305 when varying ESG bound). Preprocessing: compute expected returns vector r and covariance Σ from historical data; map integer xi to binary variables via standard binary encoding.
experiment_process: 1) Compute expected returns r and covariance Σ from historical market data. 2) Solve continuous Markowitz problem with CVXPY to obtain relative weights x_c. 3) Construct discrete Markowitz utility Qd with ϕd = ϕc / Ntot and constraints xi ∈ N, sum xi = Ntot, p^T x ≤ B (budget). 4) Encode integer variables xi into binary variables (binary encoding) and map objective + constraints into Ising/QUBO using D-Wave Ocean (Ocean handles constraint-to-penalty conversion/embedding). 5) Solve the QUBO on D-Wave quantum annealer (via Ocean / hybrid constrained solver as needed) to obtain discrete portfolio x_d. 6) Compute DESG(p=1, x_d) and enforce DESG ≤ D by repeating optimization with varying D to study ESG-constrained portfolios. 7) Compare discrete solutions to rounded continuous baseline (x_c rounded via floor/ceil by B*(x_c)_i / p_i). 8) Evaluate metrics (Euclidean distance between normalized portfolios, return and volatility positions, portfolio compositions and budget allocations). 9) Use random portfolio sampling to plot/approximate efficient frontier. Parameter sweeps: vary Ntot, ϕc, budget B, and ESG bound D. (Note: low-level annealer parameters such as anneal time, number of reads/shots, chain strength, embedding specifics are not reported.)
experiment_output: Outputs include discrete portfolio allocations x_d (integer number of shares per asset), normalized relative weights x_d / Ntot, portfolio initial value p^T x, DESG distance, and position in return-volatility space. Reported metrics: Euclidean norm || x_c - x_d ||_2 between continuous and discrete normalized allocations, return and volatility of portfolios, efficient-frontier membership (visual), and comparisons against the rounded continuous baseline (differences in return up to ~2 percentage points reported in a case). Tabulated outputs: Ntot and p^T x for different ESG bounds, per-asset counts and per-asset euro allocations for solutions.

key_findings: [supported] A discrete Markowitz portfolio theory (DMPT) with integer stock weights can be formulated and solved for realistic problem sizes using a quantum annealer (D-Wave) within a hybrid quantum-classical workflow.

[supported] The discrete risk-aversion parameter must be rescaled as ϕ_d = ϕ_c / N_tot to make discrete and continuous Markowitz formulations comparable; with this normalization the discrete solutions converge to continuous solutions as N_tot increases.

[supported] If the risk-aversion parameter is not renormalized (naive approach), discrete solutions do not converge to the continuous solution and instead converge to the minimum-variance portfolio as N_tot grows.

[supported] Introducing an explicit budget constraint and solving the discrete problem directly yields portfolios on (or near) the mean-variance efficient frontier, whereas the common procedure of rounding continuous optimal weights to integer share counts can produce visibly sub-optimal portfolios for small-to-moderate budgets.

[supported] A Wasserstein-based ESG distance (DESG) is proposed to classify portfolios by ESG performance relative to the best possible ESG portfolio; this metric generalizes the weighted-average ESG classification and can be incorporated as a linear constraint in the discrete optimization.

[supported] Applying the DESG constraint in discrete optimization progressively shifts optimal portfolios toward higher-ESG-score constituents but, as the constraint tightens, portfolios move away from the unconstrained efficient frontier (trade-off between ESG proximity and return).

[supported] Case studies (EURO STOXX 50 subset and small 4-stock universes) demonstrate the method: e.g., for budget B=100,000€ and ϕ=8 the discrete optimum (N_tot=3401) had initial value ≈99,999.87€ while the rounded continuous solution had value ≈100,006.32€ and produced a lower-than-optimal return (≈2 percentage points lower).
[supported] The DMPT single-period problem is NP-hard (cited and used as motivation), reaffirming the challenge for classical brute-force exact solutions.

[speculative] A simple upper bound estimate for qubits required for binary encoding on D-Wave is provided: N_qubit ≤ k * (log2(N_tot + 1) + 1); authors note actual hardware overheads may differ and proprietary details are not public.

[speculative] Quantum annealers (and hybrid quantum-classical workflows) are presented as a promising platform to make discrete portfolio optimization feasible in practice; the paper demonstrates feasibility on small-to-moderate problems but does not provide a rigorous advantage comparison vs classical heuristics.

[speculative] The Wasserstein-based DESG framework can be extended to heterogeneous ESG scoring systems via normalization, enabling mixing of different providers' ESG data (proposed extension, not fully explored empirically).
results_summary: The paper formulates a discrete Markowitz portfolio optimization that enforces integer share counts and an explicit budget, and demonstrates (using CVXPY for continuous baselines and a D-Wave quantum annealer for discrete optimization) that (1) the discrete risk-aversion parameter must be scaled as ϕ_d = ϕ_c / N_tot to recover continuous behavior as portfolio size grows, (2) naive rounding of continuous optimal weights to integer shares can be sub-optimal for realistic budgets while direct discrete optimization yields portfolios on the efficient frontier, and (3) a Wasserstein-distance-based ESG constraint (DESG) can be incorporated to steer optimal portfolios toward higher ESG scores at the cost of some deviation from the unconstrained efficient frontier. Experiments on small instrument universes and EURO STOXX 50 components illustrate these findings.
performance_claims: For budget B = 100000€ and risk-aversion ϕ = 8: discrete optimum with N_tot = 3401 yields initial portfolio value ≈ 99,999.87€; rounded continuous solution yields ≈ 100,006.32€ and a return ≈ 2 percentage points lower than the discrete optimum (reported as a visible sub-optimality).
In ESG-constrained experiments, the maximum reachable DESG within the chosen 4-stock investment universe was found to be 1.6 (on ISS-ESG grading scale from 4 to 1).

Table I examples: for DESG D = 1.6 → N_tot = 960 and ⃗p^T x ≈ 99,999.56€; D = 1.5 → N_tot = 1112 and ⃗p^T x ≈ 99,998.61€; D = 1.4 → N_tot = 1202 and ⃗p^T x ≈ 99,994.84€; D = 1.3 → N_tot = 1305 and ⃗p^T x ≈ 99,932.86€ (illustrating required adjustments in N_tot to fit budget while satisfying ESG constraint).
Qubit-usage upper-bound estimate: N_qubit ≤ k * (log2(N_tot + 1) + 1) (theoretical estimate for binary encoding).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper demonstrates feasibility of solving discrete portfolio optimization instances on a D-Wave quantum annealer and argues that quantum annealers are a natural choice for DMPT (Ising encoding). However, it does not present controlled runtime, scaling, or solution-quality comparisons against classical exact or heuristic methods that would establish a concrete quantum advantage; thus any claim of advantage is asserted as promising/speculative rather than demonstrated.
limitations: Reliance on historical returns and covariance data — study uses historical data and does not establish that ESG-aware constraints will improve forward-looking performance (author-stated).
Only Wasserstein p = 1 was used for the ESG distance measure; role of other p values was not explored (author-stated).
ESG data limited to a single provider (ISS ESG) and a single homogeneous scoring system for the case studies — heterogeneous / multi-provider ESG data not implemented (author-stated).
Case studies use small, restricted investment universes (examples with 4 stocks and selected EURO STOXX 50 components); scalability to large universes not demonstrated (author-stated/inferred).
Single-period (one-shot) optimization only — multi-period / dynamic portfolio problems not addressed (author-stated/inferred).
Budget and Ntot trade-off: method requires choosing Ntot and increasing it until budget is nearly exhausted; practical tuning required (author-stated/inferred).
Quantum annealer specifics and embedding overhead are proprietary/opaque: required qubit overhead and embedding details are not public and could affect scalability/performance (author-stated).
D-Wave Ocean transforms constraints/penalties in a proprietary way and current tooling does not support going beyond long-only portfolios (author-stated).
[inferred] Quantum-annealer solutions may be approximate and dependent on annealer tuning/embedding; the paper does not provide formal guarantees of global optimality for large instances.
[inferred] The work assumes static ESG scores (uses latest ESG date in the period) and does not model time-varying ESG signals or score revisions.
[inferred] Transaction costs, market impact, liquidity and other realistic trading frictions are not included in the discrete optimization formulation.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Direct discrete optimization on a D-Wave annealer outperforms naive rounding of continuous Markowitz solutions (reported improvements include up to ~2 percentage points in return and smaller Euclidean distance between normalized allocations).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrated end-to-end pipeline using D-Wave Ocean / hybrid solver and CVXPY on real market and ISS ESG data, indicating practical NISQ-era applicability for small asset universes and realistic budget constraints.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Workflow relies on classical preprocessing (expected returns/covariance computation, binary encoding of integers) and classical postprocessing, with the QUBO solved by the annealer (hybrid constrained quadratic solver referenced).

#idea:quantum-advantage — Formal discrete Markowitz (DMPT) formulation with integer share counts and a derived rescaling φ_d = φ_c / Ntot ensures discrete solutions converge to continuous ones as Ntot grows, enabling principled comparison between discrete and continuous solutions.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Novel incorporation of ESG constraints via a Wasserstein-1 distance metric (DESG) added as a linear constraint in the discrete problem, demonstrating the trade-off surface among return, risk, and ESG-friendliness on EURO STOXX 50 components.

#limitation:qubit-count — The paper omits precise QPU model, actual qubit usage, and embedding overhead; only a theoretical qubit-count estimate formula is given (Nqubit ≤ k*(log2(Ntot+1)+1)), leaving scalability to larger universes unclear.

#limitation:data-encoding — Integer-to-binary encoding is used and acknowledged to increase qubit requirements; the cost of encoding large Ntot into binary variables is a potential scaling bottleneck.

#limitation:noise — Low-level annealer parameters (anneal time, number of reads, chain strength) and any noise/embedding issues or mitigation strategies are not reported, hindering reproducibility and assessment of hardware noise impact.
